title: Agriculture
subject: geography
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Geography: 17 marks + 3 map marks). sections.title: The land that feeds a billion

blocks.title: Why is the same rice a business in Punjab and dinner in Odisha?
blocks.body:
A farmer in Punjab grows rice and sells almost all of it to government procurement centres. A farmer in Odisha grows rice too, but keeps most of it to feed the family. Same crop, two very different kinds of farming.

India is an agriculturally important country: about **two-thirds** of its population is engaged in agricultural activities. This chapter explains the types of farming, the cropping seasons, where our major crops grow, and the reforms that changed Indian agriculture.

blocks.title: The scientist who fed India
blocks.body:
In the 1960s India depended on food imports and feared famine. Agricultural scientist **M. S. Swaminathan** worked with farmers to test new **high-yielding varieties (HYV)** of wheat in Punjab and other states.

Wheat harvests soared, and India became largely self-sufficient in grain. This became known as the **Green Revolution**. Later he warned that soil and water must be protected too, calling for an 'evergreen revolution'.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in agricultural science, agronomy, food technology, horticulture and agri-business.

blocks.question: Why is rice a commercial crop in Punjab but a subsistence crop in Odisha?
options: Punjab has assured irrigation, modern inputs and access to markets; Odisha's farming is more rain-fed and for family use
blocks.explanation: The degree of commercialisation depends on irrigation, technology and markets, not just on the crop.

blocks.title: Subsistence, commercial and plantation farming
blocks.body:
Agriculture is an age-old economic activity in India. Farming varies from **subsistence to commercial** type, depending on physical environment, technology and socio-cultural practices.

**1. Primitive subsistence farming:** practised on small patches of land with **primitive tools** like the hoe, dao and digging sticks, and **family or community labour**. It depends on **monsoon**, the natural fertility of the soil and suitability of other environmental conditions. It is **'slash and burn' agriculture**: farmers clear a patch of land and produce cereals and other food crops to sustain their family. When the soil fertility decreases, farmers shift and clear a fresh patch. This allows nature to replenish the fertility of the soil through natural processes. Land productivity is low because the farmer does not use fertilisers or other modern inputs. It is known by different names in different parts of the country (see the table); in the north-eastern states it is called **jhumming**.

**2. Intensive subsistence farming:** practised in areas of **high population pressure** on land. It is **labour-intensive**, with high doses of **biochemical inputs and irrigation** for higher production. Though the 'right of inheritance' leads to the **division of land** among successive generations and makes land-holding size uneconomical, farmers continue to take maximum output from the limited land because they have no alternative source of livelihood.

**3. Commercial farming:** uses **higher doses of modern inputs**: **high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides**. The degree of commercialisation varies from region to region: for example, **rice** is a commercial crop in **Punjab and Haryana**, but in **Odisha** it is a **subsistence** crop.

**4. Plantation farming:** a type of commercial farming in which a **single crop** is grown on a **large area**. It has an interface of agriculture and industry. Plantations cover large tracts of land, use **capital-intensive inputs** and **migrant labourers**; all the produce is used as raw material in industries. Important plantation crops are **tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana**. **Tea in Assam and North Bengal** and **coffee in Karnataka** are important plantation crops. Since production is mainly for the market, a well-developed network of transport and communication connecting plantations, processing industries and markets plays an important role.

blocks.question: In which type of farming is a single crop grown on a large area for industry?
blocks.explanation: Tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana are plantation crops.
option_feedback: That grows food on small, crowded holdings.
That is small-scale, for the family.

blocks.question: What is slash-and-burn farming called in the north-eastern states?
blocks.explanation: In the north-east it is called jhumming.

blocks.title: Rabi, kharif and zaid
blocks.body:
India has three major cropping seasons.

**Rabi:** crops are sown in **winter from October to December** and harvested in **summer from April to June**. Important rabi crops are **wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard**. They are grown in large parts of India, but states from the north and north-western parts such as **Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh** are important for wheat and other rabi crops. Precipitation during winter from **western temperate cyclones** helps the success of these crops. The success of the **Green Revolution** in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan has also been important.

**Kharif:** crops are grown with the **onset of monsoon** in different parts of the country and harvested in **September-October**. Important kharif crops are **paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean**. Important rice-growing regions are **Assam, West Bengal, coastal Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra, particularly the Konkan coast**, along with **Uttar Pradesh and Bihar**; recently paddy has also become an important crop of **Punjab and Haryana**. In **Assam, West Bengal and Odisha**, **three crops of paddy** are grown in a year: **Aus, Aman and Boro**.

**Zaid:** a **short season during the summer months**, between the rabi and kharif seasons. Crops include **watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops**. **Sugarcane** takes almost a year to grow.

blocks.title: The three cropping seasons
blocks.body:
| Season | Sown | Harvested | Main crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rabi** | winter, October to December | summer, April to June | wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard |
| **Kharif** | with the onset of monsoon | September to October | paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean |
| **Zaid** | short summer season between rabi and kharif | summer | watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder crops |

blocks.question: Which crop is a rabi crop?
blocks.explanation: Wheat is sown October-December and harvested April-June.

blocks.question: Aus, Aman and Boro are three crops of paddy grown in:
blocks.explanation: Three paddy crops a year are grown there.
option_feedback: These grow one main paddy crop.
The chapter names Assam, West Bengal and Odisha.

blocks.title: Rice, wheat, millets, maize and pulses
blocks.body:
A variety of food and non-food crops are grown in different parts of India, depending on soil, climate and cultivation practices.

**Rice:** the **staple food crop** of a majority of the people in India. India is the **second largest producer of rice** in the world after **China**. It is a **kharif** crop which requires **high temperature (above 25°C)**, **high humidity** and **annual rainfall above 100 cm**; in areas of less rainfall it grows with the help of **irrigation**. Rice is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and deltaic regions. Development of a dense network of **canal irrigation and tubewells** has made it possible to grow rice in areas of less rainfall such as **Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan**.

**Wheat:** the second most important cereal crop and the main food crop in the **north and north-western** part of the country. This **rabi** crop requires a **cool growing season** and **bright sunshine at the time of ripening**, with **50 to 75 cm** of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season. There are two important wheat-growing zones: the **Ganga-Satluj plains** in the north-west and the **black soil region of the Deccan**. Major wheat-producing states are **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan**.

**Millets:** **jowar, bajra and ragi** are the important millets grown in India. Though known as **coarse grains**, they have **very high nutritional value**: ragi is very rich in **iron, calcium**, other micronutrients and roughage.
- **Jowar** is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production. It is **rain-fed**, grown mostly in moist areas, hardly needing irrigation. **Maharashtra** is the largest producer, followed by Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
- **Bajra** grows well on **sandy soils and shallow black soil**. **Rajasthan** is the largest producer, followed by Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Haryana.
- **Ragi** is a crop of **dry regions** and grows well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils. **Karnataka** is the largest producer, followed by Tamil Nadu; it is also grown in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Jharkhand and Arunachal Pradesh.

**Maize:** used both as **food and fodder**. It is a **kharif** crop which requires a temperature between **21°C and 27°C** and grows well in **old alluvial soil**; in states like **Bihar**, maize is grown in the **rabi** season too. Use of HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation has increased its production. Major states: **Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana**.

**Pulses:** India is the **largest producer as well as consumer of pulses** in the world. They are the major source of **protein** in a vegetarian diet. Major pulses are **tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram**. They need **less moisture** and survive even in dry conditions. Being **leguminous** crops, all these crops **except arhar** help in **restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air**, so they are mostly grown in **rotation** with other crops. Major pulse-producing states are **Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka**.

blocks.title: Major crops at a glance
blocks.body:
| Crop | Season | Climate and soil | Major states |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rice** | kharif | above 25°C, high humidity, rainfall above 100 cm (irrigation where less) | West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, plains of north and north-east, coastal and deltaic areas |
| **Wheat** | rabi | cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening, 50-75 cm rainfall | Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan |
| **Maize** | kharif (rabi too in Bihar) | 21°C to 27°C, old alluvial soil | Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana |
| **Sugarcane** | about a year | 21°C to 27°C, hot humid, 75-100 cm rainfall | Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana |
| **Tea** | plantation | warm, moist, frost-free; deep fertile well-drained soil rich in humus | Assam, Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri (West Bengal), Tamil Nadu, Kerala |
| **Coffee** | plantation | Arabica variety; hill slopes | Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu (Nilgiris) |
| **Rubber** | plantation | above 25°C, rainfall over 200 cm, moist and humid | Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andaman and Nicobar, Garo hills (Meghalaya) |
| **Cotton** | kharif, 6-8 months | black soil, high temperature, light rain, 210 frost-free days | Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh |
| **Jute** | kharif | fertile floodplain soils renewed every year, high temperature | West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya |

blocks.question: Which millet is very rich in iron and calcium?
blocks.explanation: Ragi is rich in iron, calcium, other micronutrients and roughage.
option_feedback: Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production.
Bajra grows on sandy and shallow black soils.
Maize is not a millet in the chapter's list.

blocks.question: Which state is the largest producer of bajra?
blocks.explanation: Bajra grows well on the sandy soils of Rajasthan.
option_feedback: Karnataka is the largest producer of ragi.
Punjab is known for wheat and rice.

blocks.title: Sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, horticulture and fibres
blocks.body:
**Sugarcane:** a tropical as well as subtropical crop. It grows well in **hot and humid climate** with a temperature of **21°C to 27°C** and annual rainfall between **75 cm and 100 cm**; irrigation is required in regions of low rainfall. It can be grown on a variety of soils and needs **manual labour** from sowing to harvesting. India is the **second largest producer of sugarcane** after **Brazil**. It is the main source of **sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses**. Major states: **Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab and Haryana**.

**Oilseeds:** different oilseeds cover about **12 per cent** of the total cropped area of the country. The main oilseeds are **groundnut, mustard, coconut, sesamum (til), soyabean, castor seeds, cotton seeds, linseed and sunflower**. Most are edible and used as cooking mediums; some are also used as raw material for soap, cosmetics and ointments. **Groundnut** is a **kharif** crop and accounts for about half of the major oilseeds produced in the country; **Gujarat** was the largest producer of groundnut, followed by Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu (2019-20). **Linseed and mustard** are **rabi** crops; **sesamum** is a **kharif crop in the north and a rabi crop in south India**; **castor seed** is grown as both rabi and kharif crop.

**Tea:** an important beverage crop introduced in India initially by the **British**. Today most tea plantations are owned by Indians. The tea plant grows well in **tropical and subtropical climates** endowed with **deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter**. Tea bushes require a **warm and moist frost-free climate** all through the year, and **frequent showers evenly distributed** over the year ensure continuous growth of tender leaves. Tea is a **labour-intensive** industry needing abundant, cheap and skilled labour; it is processed within the tea garden to keep it fresh. Major tea-producing states are **Assam, the hills of Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri districts (West Bengal), Tamil Nadu and Kerala**; also Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Andhra Pradesh and Tripura.

**Coffee:** Indian coffee is known in the world for its good quality. The **Arabica** variety, initially brought from **Yemen**, is produced in the country. Its cultivation was introduced on the **Baba Budan Hills** and even today it is confined to the **Nilgiri** in **Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu**.

**Horticulture crops:** India is a major producer of **fruits and vegetables** in the world, of both tropical and temperate varieties. Mangoes of **Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal**; oranges of **Nagpur and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya)**; bananas of **Kerala, Mizoram, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu**; lichi and guava of **Uttar Pradesh and Bihar**; pineapples of **Meghalaya**; grapes of **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra**; and apples, pears, apricots and walnuts of **Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh** are in great demand.

**Non-food crops:**
- **Rubber:** an **equatorial** crop, but under special conditions also grown in tropical and sub-tropical areas. It requires a **moist and humid climate** with **rainfall of more than 200 cm** and a **temperature above 25°C**. It is an important industrial raw material, grown mainly in **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Garo hills of Meghalaya**.
- **Fibre crops:** **cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk**. The first three come from crops grown in the soil; silk is obtained from cocoons of silkworms fed on green mulberry leaves. Rearing silkworms for silk is called **sericulture**.
- **Cotton:** India is believed to be the **original home of the cotton plant**. Cotton grows well in the drier parts of the **black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau**. It requires **high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine**. It is a **kharif** crop taking **6 to 8 months** to mature. Major states: **Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh**.
- **Jute:** known as the **golden fibre**. It grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the **flood plains where soils are renewed every year**; **high temperature** is required during growth. **West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya** are the major producers. It is used for gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn, carpets and other artefacts. Due to its high cost, it is losing the market to **synthetic fibres** and packing materials, particularly **nylon**.

blocks.question: Which crop needs more than 200 cm of rainfall and temperature above 25°C?
blocks.explanation: Rubber is an equatorial crop of moist, humid climates.

blocks.question: Why is jute called the 'golden fibre', and why is it losing its market?
options: It is used for jewellery; jewellery is out of fashion
For its golden colour and value; it is losing out to cheaper synthetic fibres like nylon
It is mined like gold; it is running out
It grows only in deserts; deserts are shrinking
blocks.explanation: Its high cost makes it lose the market to synthetic packing materials.
option_feedback: It is used for bags, mats and ropes.
Jute is a crop, not a mineral.

blocks.title: Technological and institutional reforms

blocks.question: Which is a technological reform that increased milk production?
blocks.explanation: The White Revolution boosted milk production.
option_feedback: The Green Revolution was about food grains.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Seasons: "Rabi = Rest in winter, reap in summer" (Oct–Dec → Apr–Jun); "Kharif = Comes with the monsoon"; "Zaid = Zippy summer fruits" (melons, cucumber).**
- **Largest producers: "Jowar–Maharashtra, Bajra–Rajasthan, Ragi–Karnataka" (J-M, B-R, R-K).**
- **Second after: rice after China; sugarcane after Brazil.**
- **Rainfall ladder: wheat 50-75 cm < sugarcane 75-100 cm < rice 100+ cm < rubber 200+ cm.**
- **Paddy trio in the east: "Aus, Aman, Boro".**
- **Pulses fix nitrogen, except arhar.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Calling wheat a kharif crop: it is **rabi**.
2. Saying all pulses fix nitrogen: **arhar is the exception**.
3. Saying India is the largest producer of rice: it is **second after China** (and second in sugarcane after Brazil).
4. Mixing up jowar (Maharashtra), bajra (Rajasthan) and ragi (Karnataka).
5. Saying coffee in India is Robusta from Brazil: the chapter's variety is **Arabica from Yemen**, first grown on the **Baba Budan Hills**.
6. Saying cotton needs heavy rain: it needs **light rainfall or irrigation**, high temperature and **210 frost-free days**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Give each group a calendar and crop cards. Students place each crop in its sowing and harvesting months, then colour the rabi, kharif and zaid seasons. Next, on an outline map, mark the largest producer states of jowar, bajra, ragi, sugarcane, tea, coffee, rubber and jute.

blocks.body: A farmer with two acres keeps dividing land among children. Explain how this affects farming, and suggest one institutional reform that could help.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
Explain why rice is a commercial crop in Punjab and Haryana but a subsistence crop in Odisha (2025-26 sample paper idea), in about 100 words.

**Model answer:** Climate and irrigation: Punjab and Haryana have well-developed canal and tubewell irrigation, which allows large-scale rice cultivation even with less rain, and HYV seeds suit the area. Odisha's rice is mostly rain-fed, grown in a monsoonal climate without large irrigation systems. Economic factors: Punjab and Haryana have government procurement, good transport and access to national markets, so farmers grow rice for sale; in Odisha, rice is grown mainly for family and local use. Farming practices: Punjab and Haryana use machinery, fertilisers and modern techniques, while Odisha's farming is more traditional.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Types of farming: primitive subsistence (slash and burn, jhumming), intensive subsistence, commercial and plantation.
- Cropping seasons: rabi (wheat, mustard), kharif (rice, cotton, jute) and zaid (melons, vegetables).
- Rice needs heat, humidity and 100+ cm rain; wheat needs a cool season and 50-75 cm rain; millets are nutritious coarse grains; India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses.
- Sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee and horticulture crops; rubber, cotton and jute are important non-food crops.
- Reforms: land reforms, Green and White Revolutions, crop insurance, Grameen banks, KCC, MSP and the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper asked why rice is commercial in Haryana and Punjab but subsistence in Odisha (2 marks: at least one climate point and one economic point).
- 3/5-mark favourites: types of farming, cropping seasons, conditions for rice, wheat, tea, sugarcane, cotton and jute, and reforms.
- **Map work:** major rice and wheat areas, and the largest or major producer states of sugarcane, tea, coffee, rubber, cotton and jute.

blocks.front: Name the three cropping seasons and one crop each.
blocks.back: Rabi: wheat. Kharif: rice. Zaid: watermelon.
Warm, moist, frost-free climate; frequent, evenly distributed showers; deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus; cheap skilled labour.

blocks.front: Why are pulses grown in rotation?
blocks.back: Being leguminous (except arhar), they fix nitrogen from the air and restore soil fertility.
Vinoba Bhave's movement in which landowners gifted land (Bhoodan) or whole villages (Gramdan) to the landless: a 'blood-less revolution'.
